They also have an amazing bonsai garden and a lovely water garden.I spent almost 2 hours exploring the flora on well marked walkways and paths in this lovely park.BTW, Hallim deserves an entrance fee for all the upkeep needed, not sure why they charge 2 dollars at a number of sea cliffs etc., that should be open to the public...

With an entrance fee of 10,000 KRW (considered high for local attractions), my high expectations was quickly grounded with its shallow presentation of regional fauna. If you're from the tropics (like me), the Subtropical Botanic Garden (common palms, bananas, Bougainvillea etc) is a major yawn fest. There was a Wild Grass and Flower section which, in the absence of signage, could be easily mistaken by anyone to be a neglected zone in the Park. We skipped 2 other zones and zoomed in on the other highlights. The Caves were fine but nothing very impressive - tiny (imagine your pinke. Halve it) stalactites and stalagmites with their equally tiny rain parade could do no more to dampen your spirits than the Park already had. Saving grace come in the form of a cutest piglet that was a pet of the owner of Macaw House (warning: there is a separate entrance fee of 1000 KRW for this attraction) though I doubt it'll stay this cute for long. If you are visiting in Apr, then the Cherry Blossoms section would be opened but  the question is why you would pay 10,000 KRW for something that would be free all over the island.

Hallim Park offers a quiet getaway from the big city noise.  For only 9.00 US you can spend 2-5 hours strolling through the different gardens,see the birds, and in April see the tulips and cherry tree blossoms.   A great place to bring kids as they can walk through the cool caves, and stone gardens.   Everything was well labeled in English and well laid out.   Heyopjae Beach is across the street where you can have a picnic or can buy food in the park.  The paths would be easy for strollers or wheelchairs.   After spending to much on waterfalls and cheesy museums, this was a special treat.   Go early in the day to avoid the tourist buses or school groups.
Has a little bit of eveything that Jeju offers, lots of trees, flowers, stones, caves and a tiny folk village.

Nice place to have a relaxing walk with lots of trees and plants. If you are there try to visit the herbal cafe with the ostrich and peacocks just beside it, it was very nice having a cup of tea there.

We loved walking through Halla Park. The paths are organized and cultured so beautifully. Every turn brings new surprises. There are bonsai trees galore, rock formations, fountains, and green spaces the lure you in. The caves are small, but fascinating. The birds here are delightful, from parakeets to peacocks and ostriches. We would definitely come back and have a picnic here in the springtime.
The park has different areas including water garden, bird garden, bonsai garden, cave and folk village... Overall, the garden is very nice, huge but the entrance ticket is a bit bit bit pricey.

Hallim Park has a mixed big of attractions --- from folk village, lava cave to bonsai and tropical gardens.  It is worth spending a couple of hours exploring.......many nice spots for taking pictures around the park........beware though, each of the attraction is not very spectacular or unique, but the park just gives a sense of the essentials in Jeju in one place
It's worth visiting. Beautiful nature. You need about two hours for this. There is also nice beach near the park.
Beautiful, clean and very well maintained. It has great collection of plants, cactus etc. Beautiful cave and water garden too. Should allocate 3 hours time to enjoy this place.
It was a nice mix of gardens, animals, nature (caves).  Good for families.  Not great in anything but a good variety to keep everyone interested.

This park provides a pleasant, albeit uninspiring, afternoon. It's across from a pretty beach, has some nice landscaping, a sampling of lava tubes, and a some nice gardens. I wouldn't recommend driving all the way to the west side of the island just to visit Hallim, but if you're in the area, it's worth a few hours.
There were so many beautiful flower like sakuram dafodil etc, something you can see without having to visit the original country. Everything were so beautiful!
Take the afternoon and walk around this beautiful park and zoo. All different kind of plants, trees, flowers, and animals, this park is way better than it seems. Don't miss it!

It's the first stop in our itinerary & we went to the Ssanyong cave where there are also lava tubes. It's not as big  as Manjang cave & it's better lighted. There's also a folk village in this park, a flower & bonsai garden & lots of lava stones formed into different figures. A bird sanctuary is also here.
This place was really pretty (though remote) close to Hyeopjae beach on Jeju's west coast. Really pretty, reasonably priced and lots to see. Would recommend to couples and families especially.

We visited Hallim Park with my daughter in August. It is very nice place with diversified trees, plants, birds. Convenient infrastructure allowed us to see so many wonderful natural things during three hours. Two old cave are in the park. It is interesting to pass them especially in hot day.

A nice place to go for a couple of hours if you like animals and botany but in my opinion it was too expensive at 9000 Won per person. I think a fair price would be 6000 Won per person especially as the food and drink inside the park was extremely expensive.

I visited Hallim Park confined in a wheelchair. Some ways are not appropiate for a wheelchair. I love gardens and seen a lot. This garden had beautiful displays although some were needing care. The park takes several hours to see. It has different plants from many parts of the word. The Bonsai collection was excellent and one of the best I seen in a botanical garden. Again this particular area was needing help with the trees. They have so many bonsais and only two workers to trim them. And the specimens available were very old.The caves are unique because I do not know any other part in the world you can see a volcanical and calcareal cave together and they have one in here. I had to use crutches to see them and I am not dissapointed of the effort.The local village moved into the park is nice and realistic (we visited a folk village the day before). The animal collection was above average. For kids they have an area to feed love birds and parakeets. Excellent fun. My youngest daughter is 25 and she was a child again in here.

This park has it all - Plants, bonsai, trees, birds, ostriches, stone sculptures, lava caves, folk houses. However, it is really big so you might need to have more than 3 hours to finish the entire park.
lots of nice trees, bonsais, stones & cave. This Park was made by one man alone

Hallim Park features an extremely interesting cave complex quite unique as it has been dug by lava, a traditional Korean village, beautiful waterfalls, a bonsai garden and a section with creative sculptures. The price is very affordable and you can also visit the beautiful beach opposite the park while you're there. Worth a visit if you have spare time on your hands as it is quite far from the main attractions.
There are lots of things to see here, we spend 2 hours here. Beautiful trees, caves, stones, small waterfall. It is all about nature and traditional korea living.

Garden full of flower aroma when flower blossom session. Overall not very attractive. A common/general attraction with combination theme. Good for family outing. You may buy Jeju chocolate with different flavor. Its really taste nice. If you worry about the quality, free tasting available.

So much to offer from beautiful botanic displays to a fabulous Bonsai area which was so peaceful and various specimens of fauna.... Plus several species of cacti. Caves to go down and lovely park area..... A lovely outing which was also very reasonably priced.
A beautiful garden for those who nature lover. Don't forget to bring camera or video cam.

I am not overly interested in much to with botany but if I were I think I would have enjoyed this park much more. (We were also there in late January so Im not sure how much the park differs in the warmer seasons)We had nothing planned for the day and happened upon Hallim Park when we were wondering around aimlessly so it filled its purpose to us as something to do/see for 1-2 hours time.The park displays plant (and some animal) species from Korea but mostly imported from other regions in a very touristy manner. It also provides easy access to some lava tubes/caves with a paved walkway through them that are somewhat interesting as well as some other themed areas.I wouldn't go out of your way to visit this park but if you in the area its an alright place to kill some time. (unless you a botanist then I'm sure you'd enjoy it much more)- there were some ostriches that were pecking out their/each others feathers which wasn't the most pleasant state to see them in but they were at least provided with decent space to roam9,000 won/pp in January 2012

It smells so good as soon as you get off the car and pass the entrance. After a short walk, you get to the Forest.  It is also easily accessible for baby strollers as they put some straw mats alone the forest so the whole family can enjoy a wonderful walk in the forest.  Not sure if wheelchairs can roll easily on those mats though but I saw quite some baby strollers.We took a detour after Sangumburi crater (about 20 min away), and spent about an hour in the forest but didn't complete it. Then in another 20-30 min, we arrived at a Five Day Market, which is about 10 min from the Haeyeo (Women Divers) museum.So this was how we planned our route to and from the forest.

I found much of Jeju island to be very commercialized and crowded with loud tour groups. This is a great place to enjoy the natural beaty of Jeju with smaller groups of people. There is a small entrance fee.  The first half mile is along a wide crushed rock road. It is lined with young "nutmeg" trees. The trees are in the yew family. They are Torreya nucifera and are native to Japan. I  visited in October when the small edible nuts ripen. The nuts are encased in a thin husk that has a wonderful aroma. You will see people collecting them under the large trees.  Eventually the road ends and then you follow a loop trail that is about 2 feet wide it is covered with a hemp rope mat that felt lovely to walk on with bare feet.  The crowds end at the beginning of the narrow trail so you can walk through this section in peace and really marvel at the enchanting colors and smells of the forest and hear the songs of the many birds.  There were signs to watch for snakes but I saw none. The yews are huge.  Make sure to investigate the tree bark it is fabric like and soft. Also many of the other plants have English name labels which is nice. The trail is flat and should take a leisurely couple of hours or less if you rush.  I noticed a lot of people sitting on benches in the first section enjoying picnic lunches.

This forest is peaceful, gorgeous, and sit you shouldn't skip. You can get here by car (if you brought one) taxi, or by taking several buses. You can take a map with you but you shouldn't get lost its all marked and one loooooong path. This takes a whole day if you plan to make it to the end. We didn't because we came in the afternoon and didn't want to be in the dark trying to find our way back. It is humid so dress light in summer, and bring water.Don't forget to bring a camera as there are beautiful natural rock formations and plant life, as well as bridges to pose on and if you are lucky you'll see Jeju deer frolicking around. We were super lucky and saw 4! There are little "rest stops" along the way but they are like camping ground logs to sit on and Korean squatter outhouses. The only problem I had was the bathrooms....I just couldn't bring myself to go because one they were smelly, two they were dark, three filled with various spiders and I was too terrified to go. If you are brave enough bring tissue paper you wipe with and to toss into the trash. (Tip many bathrooms in Korea don't have toilet paper in the stall. You have to grab it by the sinks before you head in. Many Koreans carry tissues in their purses or bags in case a bathroom is out of tissue. Be wise. Carry tissue. It can save you from an embarrassing episode)We want to go again so we can at least get to the prehistoric volcanic rock formation that we hear have lush plant life all around it!

Bijarim Forest is one of the most visited attractions in Gujwa area.  The forest area is quite small and walkable in about a half hour.  The fauna there isn t anything out of the ordinary but the walk was pleasant especially in the hot weather when all of the path is in shaded areas.  I m not sure why the forest gets so many visitors, especially with the 3000 won charge (which is probably necessary to control the number of visitors) as an area like this can be found in some public parks that are free.  Since there is really only one path, it s impossible to avoid other tourists making it impossible to have a peaceful time.

We visited this place on a slightly gloomy day. This and the amazon green colours of the flora made it look like a mystic forest, something out of an animation. They say, walking among these nutmeg trees has healing properties, and eventhough I was sceptical at first, soon I could feel my nerves calming down. It felt like someone poured some sleeping powder on us. Oh and the smell! I've never felt such pungent yet clean fragrance in a forest before, it's truly unique. All those pretty colours and the distinctive smell of nutmeg and cinnamon trees makes this pathway a mesmerizing experience. The route takes at least 40 minutes-1 hour. There are some charming restaurants and coffee places before the entrance, and a huge parking lot. The whole are is beautiful.

Perfect for couples to take a romantic walk through the woods. Be sure to take the shortcut if you just want to get to the end of it quickly and see the oldest tree around, or if you're a romantic be sure to take the long route and walk hand in hand with your beloved. Enjoyed the refreshing walk and highly recommended.

We went there right after rain, which is a recommended time to visit since there are more fresh air pumping out from all those trees. The view reminded me of Totoro, the mysterious forest atmosphere!! I would definately visit again.

If you want to enjoy around two hours walking without difficulties in the middle of an amazing and dense  forest I highly recommend you to visit Bijarim. Considering the time needed for these trees (nutmeg yew, family of the Taxus) to grow and the fact that normally you can only find it as bushes into other species's forest this place is a unique jewel with many of the trees aging more that 500 or indeed 800 years. Beautiful and relaxing experience that I will keep forever in my memories as a lover of trees that I am.

The way to Bija Forest is very peaceful and beautiful. I think it is better to go during lunch time because it is less people. It takes 40 mins to walk and super easy. I saw many families with all different ages. It doesn't matter how fit you are, and I think anyone can walk on the trail. (I even saw several girls with high heels) There are several good photo spots as well. Walking on the forest was refreshing and relaxing. I hiked Mountain Halla a day before and it helped me to recover from 9 hours of walk.

We visited this place out of curiosity and was quite surprised how peaceful it was. It was a weekday when we were there but it might get a lot more crowded on weekends.Give this place a chance if you would like to experience a walk, albeit on man made trails, in the forest as it was quiet, peaceful and there are many great photo ops.
A lovely nature-based walk in a beautiful forest. Appreciating the history and beauty of these ancient nutmeg trees!
Good place to have a relaxing walk in a natural forest. It's not a long hike, about an hour, and there are flat trails. Check out the cafe that has nice tea beside the car park.

The visit to Bijarim Forest is a relaxing visit with a closer touch to the nature, feeling calm and peace. The trees looks aged and birds chirping, soft wind blowing. There are many locals walking or jogging in the forest during my visit. I would love to revisit it again if I visit Jeju again.

Carpark available. It was a lovely walk in the forest. Wear comfortable shoes and a light jacket. We went during autumn. I have sinus.. but minute we walked into the forest, my nose magically cleared up. The air was fresh and the sounds in the forest was beautiful. Wish i could record it. They have created a path to walk so its easy. No food allowed though. Took about an hour to walk.
Really nice for walking. Quiet, peaceful and quaint place. It is good place to rest from cities and people.

My family and both of my grandmas said they felt like they gained 10 years more of their life after walking through this forest. The trails are excellent and there s plenty to see for all ages. Definitely one of the prettiest sights of Jeju.

Came here for a leisure stroll after a heavy breakfast. Air was fresh and cool. Would be better if it was quiet but there are a number of tour groups with speakers and people talkin loudly. Kinda disturb the tranquility associated with the place

If you need a good work out, this forest in Jeju is worth paying a visit. The autumn 10C air is perfect, although the leaves were only starting to blend with the sun, you can imagine the shades of red, orange and yellow if it's at its peak!  The old nutmeg trees provided good photo opportunities for those with a passion for nature.
Great to go for a stroll through the forrest. Either early morning or late afternoon would be perfect

I am really amazed and really love walking inside the forest you will feel delighted very clean and green trees, smells good and you can relax and breath well. Bijarim Forest-Is a group of about 2,800 nutmeg trees between 500 and 800 years old. They are 7-14m in height and 50-110cm in diameter. This is the largest nutmeg tree forest in the world. In the middle of the forest is an 800-year-old tree, called  Ancestor tree of the Bija trees.

This place will be good for nature lovers and those who are in Jeju to relax and get away from busy city life. It only takes 1hour to cover the area at a slow pace. You may get a chance to see autumn foliage here from mid to late Nov as there are quite a number of maple trees in the forest. (Note: Autumn is mild in Jeju, while northern parts of Korea are having colourful autumn foliage, we hardly see any colourful trees in Jeju till we came to Bijarim forest)

It was once the most beautiful street in Korea. As a German that comes from the countryside it was just a regular forest with a small hiking trail. Nothing real special about. I was a little disappointed.If you're in a hurry, don't visit the Bijarim Forest but rather the Lava tunnel which is close by!

A lot of tourists about. This was a small park but it seemed quite popular. But my preference would be the village where they shot the korean series 'the legend'. Just can't remember the name of the village. Anyways I was here around 2008. Enjoyed my tour trip

It took us less than one hour to walk around the forest. Not a bad stopover but nothing special. There is a more than 800 year old nutmeg tree in the back of the forest that represents the strong spirit of the Jeju people. Trail easy for all ages.

We took a relaxing stroll through a beautiful forest Bijraim Nutmeg Forest. The shade of the forest is perfect for a hot summer day. It's a beautiful small forest, but getting there was a bit time-consuming, involving a bus ride from Jeju City and some brief hitch-hiking. (We were to take a second bus, but we waited so long that decided to hitch a ride instead.) However, from Bijraim, there is a bus that takes you directly to the popular Manjanggul, so it's a good idea to visit both in the same day.

The world's largest nutmeg forest can be found on Jeju Island, South Korea.  A beautiful, old growth forest with a gigantic nutmeg tree as the central attraction, this forest offers quiet beauty to stroll through in a relaxed and rejuvenating atmosphere. The smell of nutmeg is distinct immediately upon entering.  Parts of the forest have beautiful red crushed stone walking paths and other parts have very well maintained wooden pathways.  To do the whole forest takes about 60 minutes at a comfortable pace.  Picture opportunities abound, and you'll likely be able to see wedding couples posing for their formal pictures amidst the beauty of the forest surroundings.  A great break from the hustle-bustle of other attractions, this forest offers the opportunity to enjoy nature in a very unique way.

This forest has a nutmeg tree that is over 826 years old.  We enjoyed walking on the paths that weave through the forest.  Beautiful trees, flowers and lovely singing birds.  We saw a snake and loved the fresh smelling air.  There is a small store selling drinks and snacks and a small coffee shop.  No gift shop.  The paths are well maintained and very easy to walk on.
It's a nice place for a walk. Very calming. You can even trek when you are deeper into the walk. Nice surroundings

Went there after visiting the Manjanggul caves, fairly close by. Not necessarily a tourist attraction, but if you're looking to spend an hour or two in a nice forest away from all the coach visitors, this is a great spot. All we saw were Koreans out for a Sunday walk. There is a circuit path through the forest, all level, well maintained, took us maybe an hour to complete. Totally relaxing and peaceful.

One of the most relaxing forests I have ever visited in Korea. Even though there were quite a lot of people around the entrance, once you go in, you feel isolated and alone surrounded by nature. The smells, sounds and views are just incredible. Come if you like nature #＿＿αメ＿결＿–듄＿녁＿ めメ＿ め솽＿ #wellnesskorea #wellnesstourismsupporters #＿■メ＿ ⓤ＿ めメ＿ め솽＿ ⒰솽＿
There are some forests that are a bit more special on the island in my opinion. But this was a lovely hourlong walk that was easy and perfect for my five year old.

It took a little over 2 hours by bus to get here. I feel conflicted with it, as a part of me liked the place but another part of me thought there was (yet again!) nothing special here. Plus the journey to get there was already exhausting so probably my feet were already asleep halfway into my walk.So only go if you can rent a car, it will take much less time to get here. All in all a relaxing place to take a stroll or read in.

The footpaths were well-marked and easy to walk even for my 71-year-old mum. I enjoyed the walk and the fresh air. The only downside was there were a few noisy tourists around so it was not so calming an experience.

This place is ok if you have some spare time and want a peaceful walk.As long as you don't meet any tours because they can me noisy.Its nothing special just trees and very little else.Not worth it if you have to come out of your way.

It s a place must visit in Jeju island. Air is so fresh and the walk is tranquil. When you walk through the forest and appreciate wat the Korean say that it is a place for meditation. There is a tap near the entrance, water is so refreshing. Trees in the forest have been there for hundred of years . It s a treat to see some trees with autumn leaves. There are some Low walls with black stone formations which apparently is the volcanic rock from Jeju itself.. Would definitely come back here again to spend more time in the forest At the end of the walk they even have the vacuum facility to blow off the red soil from your shoes

Jeju has many beautiful bushland and park areas that are truely outstanding at all seasons of the year. Bijarim Forest is yet another one of these and can be different in each of the seasons. Take water if in summer and a coat if in winter!! Enjoy wandering the pathways and seating areas provided to take in the beauty.

A pleasant walk among trees and nature. Many small flies hovering around at certain areas. A small cafe and convenience store near the entrance. An easy outing for elderly folks and a pleasant walk for families.

This is a great place to go inside the city to get some quality exercise. The trails are in great shape and the views are magical.Going for a walk is easy and fun. Finding a parking spot is a little more challenging. This is inside the city so it is a very popular spot. Great for the whole family.

Our guide brought us there and we really enjoyed walking in the park. My son was walking quietly by himself taking in the fresh air. Lovely place to find peace and tranquility and to just be in tune with yourself and nature.Lovely old nutmeg trees which give out a lovely fragrance! I could come here to walk every day!

Before, people usually visited there for watching trees, feeling energy from the forest and healing. But these days there are more and more people to take photos for wedding. Wedding couples turned into one of the enjoyments of the forest. You can go there with your family and any kind of carrier will be fine.
Nice forest but nothing incredible or uniqueThere is only one type of tree but then it is just a forest
Once you stepped in , you will feel immidate relaxation! The smell is different, the surrounding sounds quieted down and just a overall sense of calmness washing over you.

If you love nature and taking walks, you'd enjoy this place. The smell is nice and the trees are impressive, but walking around for an hour looking at hundreds of the same trees doesn't excite me. It was nice and an okay way to kill an hour, but if it's between this and doing something else, choose the ladder.
Beautiful little forest on the island. Very peaceful spot for a nice walk in good company. You can also have picnic there if you wish to.

Bijarim Forest holds about 2,800 nutmeg trees between 500 and 800 years old and is supposedly the largest nutmeg grove in the world. A 813 years old "Ancestor tree of Bijia tree", also dubbed the "New Millennium Nutmeg" (#0001 tree) sits in the middle of the forest. Local residents hope the spiritual power of this noble tree will bring happiness, prosperity, and health to all in the coming millennium.The trees emit phytoncide, said to strengthen one's immunity system and enhances natural healing of the human body. Japanese and Koreans advocate forest bathing, aka shinrin-yoku or 汝役 and sanlimyok –곕┝ respectively.  Essentially this is a short, leisurely visit to absorb the forest atmosphere and was developed in Japan during the 1980s as part of preventive health care and healing.  So do walk slowly, breathe deeply, open all your senses in the revitalising woods to calm, rejuvenate and restore your body.  Truly pleasant stroll for nature lovers and family outing.Note: Despite its charm, Bijarim Forest is more popular with locals than foreign tourists due to public transportation and lack of awareness. Cover this place as part of  Manjanggul caves/Sangumburi crater tour. The woods can get mud-logged after rainfall.
Not a big forest and you have to pay a small fee to enter, a quick hours stroll some pretty trees not much else to see though.

Not too impressed with the attraction. Went on a Monday just after a morning drizzle. Just a pretty run of the mill forest (seen waaay more impressive ones elsewhere). Doesn't help that you have to pay to get in. Be prepared to get your shoes/feet muddied.

Nothing really special. 1000 (for youth) and 2000 (adult) admission fee. I wouldn't go there if it wouldn't be close to my guesthouse.Maybe it would be interesting for families with small children. But for a walk i would rather prefer going to the beach.
You can walk around under the shade of thick netmeg trees. Also, you can enjoy basking in the woods. The oldest tree is about eight hundred and fifty years old.
Lot of trees. Fresh air. Nice walk. Most of the trees are old and have description in Korean . It has oldest nutmeg tree. Can hear lot of different birds. Love nature then must see.

This forest of nutmeg trees are easily accessible and very easy and nice to take a walk - 2 easy trails which are around 1 to 2.2 km long - all easy terrain, just some stretches of little gravel roads. We enjoyed an hour's walk in the sunset and loved it. While travelling there, keep looking out for the road which is flanked by giant nutmeg trees, said to be filming location for several Korean romantic drama.
Coming to this place in a cool weather will be really nice~ Do not need to rush, just take your time and enjoy~

We took a nice walk through the nutmeg forest, took us about an hour to finish the circuit. It isn't easy to get to if you don't have a car though-we took a taxi from manjangul lava caves, but found it very hard to get back, since there were no taxis or regular buses. Thankfully some helpful Koreans helped call a taxi for us.
This is a really beautiful stroll through the forrest but no more than that. If you're in the area and able go visit otherwise it is one of those sights you can skip if time is limited.
Winter only can see tress .Its better to visit during Spring & Autumn on blooming of flowers. Nothing mch to see.
Enjoyed the cool air, the lovely outdoor smell of nature and that it was not at all a long walk through the forest. Well tethered and constructed pathways.

Seongpanak Trail is about 9.7 km to and from the parking lot.  Few kilometers from the summit was easy with boardwalk paths and steps. I've climbed Hallasan twice now, once in December and once in early March, and both times I took this route. This route is slightly longer than Gwaneumsa, but it's also a gradual incline with several easy portions. I took this route primarily because there is not a lot of public transportation available to/from the Gwaneumsa trail, plus I'm not sure I can do a steep incline the entire way up to the summit. For Seongpanak, you have about 5 km that are easy, 2.5 km that get harder, and then a pretty brutal last 2 km. Regardless, know that there are other hiking trails around the island and even around the volcano, but only the two mentioned above will lead you all the way up to the summit.Given some of the reviews I saw that are either inaccurate or not very helpful, I hope to compile a quick list to help you decide if this is something you want to do and if so, what you will need:1) It's definitely going to be an all-day kind of thing. You will be tired afterward, so you likely won't want to schedule too many other activities for the evening. Also, it's likely that you will be sore and tired the next day or two. 2) You need to start climbing no later than 8:30 AM. As several people have mentioned, you will not be allowed to access the last chunk of the way if you're not at the second shelter by 12:30 PM (this is winter time, so the schedule varies slightly from season to season... always check the Korean tourism sites).3) Even if it's sunny, there's a chance you might need crampons. In the winter months you will need them for sure, but even last weekend people were sliding down and falling repeatedly without them. I hear that it's even worse on the Gwaneumsa trail since it's a lot more shielded from the sunshine. 4) Bring food and water! The only place you can buy something is at the very beginning of the trail, and even then the options aren't fantastic. A little protein or fruit will go a long way whenever you're starting to feel tired, and it'll help you push through. Please make sure you do not leave any of your trash along the way; there are zero trashcans, so if you carry something particularly messy, you might want to pack a bag for the waste.5) Do not use the toilet in the first shelter! It's the worst smelling bathroom ever, which is rare for Korea since things are usually so clean... I suppose it's the septic system. I suggest using the toilets at the parking lot and at the last shelter (there are two). The first one is seriously a nightmare. 6) It's not an easy hike, but it's doable even for people who don't exercise strenuously. I've seen people carrying babies all the way to the top, and I've seen small children and old people make it, too. Definitely wear the right clothing, though, and especially the right shoes. If you're hiking at a time without snow, you will spend hours circumventing rocks of all sizes and ankle support will be extremely helpful for this. Anyway, thanks for reading, I hope you have a fantastic hike!

This is the best track if you are planning to climb mount hallasan. From Jeju you take bus number 780 to Mount hallasan. Cost of taxi is around KRW17,000. To reach on the top of the mountain, it takes 4 hours. There are a lot of facilities on the way to Mount Hallasan such as toilet and place to sleep.

We did the Gwaneumsa trail up Mount Hallasan to the peak and back is over 18 miles round trip, over 3500 feet of climbing and then descending it. But it's worth it. I offer only a few points of advice. It is tougher, 800m longer, but more scenic than the Seongpanak trail. To find the Gwanmeusa trail entrance parking lot, plug in the number for the Unesco Hallasa Gwaneumsa Office: +82-64-756-9950 (you only need the last 7 digits on Jeju GPS systems if driving).1) Be prepared with good hiking and walking shoes. We saw two shoes blow out, one about 2.5 hours in. The poor guy had to walk back. There is no rescue if this happens. Also, a girl's shoe blew out on the way down about 3/4 way down, it still nearly 1.5 hours to the end depending on how slow you go. I will discuss in #3 why good shoes are so important.2) Go early, and go slow if you are not in shape or do not do activities often. Hallasan is definitely attainable by nearly anyone but it is tough, very tough because of the steep steps. Unless you are in shape and do many physical activities all the time, I recommend starting at 6AM. You MUST be at Samgakbong shelter by 12:30PM otherwise they will turn you around. It is 3/4 way up the climb. From here it is another 2 hours to the peak of the Halla.3. The volcanic stone paths and the stairs will make your legs very very tired and your feet sore. I believe they made Gwanmeusa trail challenging with rocks on purpose. These are not small rocks, they are big ones that challenge each step. Walking sticks are highly recommended. The stones seem pretty and authentic until halfway up then they are tough. Then on the way down, each step seems like a sadistic joke played by the planners. Eventually you will be relieved to make it to the bottom to your car or bus.4. Be prepared for wind. We got lucky and it was warm the day we went... in fact low warm temperatures will seem even warmer due to humidity about 1/2 the time up the mountain and back. It is a little cooler and windier at the top. Wear light, polyester clothing in layers. long sleeve tech shirt, with light jacket and light rain cover. You should be OK. Gloves and hat or scarves during cooler time. Very light during summer due to heat and humidity.After you get down on Gwanmeusa trail, there is a small restaurant with Korean snacks like pajeon and gimbap, as well as a 7/11 next door. Drink some local mokkoli or soju with with the hot snacks/food! We had a great time. Only 20 minutes out Jeju City when there is no traffic. However with rush hour traffic, or busy time it takes about 45 minutes to get back into Jeju City.

One of the most popular trails in Hallasan National Park.To get here, take bus 781 from Jeju City. The fare was 1 800 KRW (the driver can give change). The journey is about 40 minutes. The stops are announced in English. The stop is Seongpanak.Set out early as you have reach Jindallaebat shelter by 1 pm in summer (12 pm in winter). Otherwise you wouldn't be allowed to reach the summit.The trail is 9,6 km long (one way), about 4,5 hours without breaks. The trail is in some parts very ROCKY so good hiking shoes and walking holes are strongly recommended. Don't worry you wouldn't climb alone. A lot of Korean will be faster than you.The view on the summit is well worth and rewarding.Bring water and sun block.You can buy a certificate for 1 000 KRW.

This was a really enjoyable hike up the highest mountain in South Korea @ 1950m, and I recommend it as a great experience of the outdoors and physical activity.  However I saw a lot of people (both locals and foreigners) struggling with various aspects so please take note of the following points:WEATHER:  If you have the flexibility of several days from which to select, review the weather in advance and aim to choose the best day.....otherwise for example you may have no views when you emerge from the trees and at the summit.TIME, PACE & TIME-LIMITS:  This is a long hike, 19.2km round trip to be exact or about 12 miles, but is a relatively gentle incline.  The general consensus in many reviews is that it should take 10 hours total including breaks and lunch.  I would consider myself slightly above average fitness and took 6 hours total, however being solo it makes a difference because I could walk at my own brisk pace and take breaks (typically quite short 5-10 mins) when I wanted.  There are 2 shelters (with toilets) on the route located at approx 4km and 7km, and it's very important to note that for safety reasons they do not allow anyone past the second shelter (which is 2.3km from the summit) AFTER 13-00 HRS, no exceptions.  Furthermore everyone must depart the summit to start descending by 14-30 HRS latest.  I did come across quite people between the 2 shelters who appeared to be rushing to make the 13-00 deadline.  This is not recommended because either you could push yourself too hard and get exhausted, or get injured walking on the rocks, or simply miss the deadline.  FOOTWEAR:  At minimum bring sturdy training or trekking shoes, preferably hiking boots to provide ankle support. Some sections of the hike are on hessian mats and wooden walk ways which of course are very nice to walk on, however probably 30% or more is on large volcanic rocks which are not comfortable to walk on and requires some focus and concentration (especially descending when your legs are tired).  I was surprised to see some walking in sandals and they suffered.  A walking stick can be helpful but is not essential.DAYPACK:  Bring a small daypack to carry water, snacks, clothes etc and to keep your hands free.  Even in summer bring a light jacket or sweater because it can get cool at the top with the wind and elevation.  In Winter I'm sure it's really cold at the summit.PROTECTION:  Bring a hat for the higher elevations (when not in the forest), sun cream and lip balm.HYDRATION/SNACKS:  There is reportedly a source of mountain water half way up but personally I did not see it near the sign, and staff at one of the shelters advised me that no water is available.  Hence suggest that you bring at least 3-4 bottles of water or isotonic drink in your day pack per person (maybe 1.5 to 2 litres), and be sure to conserve it wisely because you'll need some on the way down.  I encountered some people on the way up who had no water left.  Muesli bars, chocolate and fruit are good sources of energy.  As well as fruit, the locals tend to pack rice & meat lunches and have communal picnics at the summit.TRANSPORT:  I used a rental car and got there early, before 8am.  The car park was already full and people started parking on both sides of the main road, which is allowed.  The bus stops are right there beside the car park for those using public transport.CERTIFICATE:   There is small office hidden away near the Seongpanak car park which will print your name on a nice certificate for 1000 Won. (US$1).IN SUMMARY: Please take the time to prepare properly and get there reasonably early so that you can enjoy the hike at your own pace.  During the walk I saw several deer, lots of beautiful butterflies and other insects and loved the great views ....Jeju is covered in 300+ volcanic cones so its amazing to see all of these.  HAVE A GREAT DAY ON HALLASAN!

TLDR:Long hike, not that easy if you're not fit. 8-9 hours, 19.6km in total.Bring at least 3L of water each. They do sell water at the checkpoint, though only in 600ml bottles.Wear shoes with good sole and ankle protectionConsider taking a small towel (or two) to wipe away sweatBring a warm jumper and possibly a clean, dry shirt. Even in summer it's cold at the topStart the hike before 8.30am if you want to reach the peak because if you don't make it past the checkpoint at around 7km in, before 12.30pm, you won't be allowed to go to the peak.Bring a plastic bag for your rubbish because there are no bins at all on the hikeFor those who want moreRemember that this hike is longer than an average work day and you will need to replace water lost through sweat. Pack around 3L of water per person. Also pack some protein and carbohydrate heavy snacks such as nuts and dried fruits to keep up your energy levels. If you sweat a lot, consider bringing an electrolyte drink sachet to use halfway (or buy a can of Pocari sweat at the checkpoint). At the checkpoint, you can buy instant noodles, 600mL water bottles and Pocari sweat. If you don't want noodles for lunch, bring lunch. But keep in mind it's cold at the top so some warm noodles can be perfect. The noodles are a bit spicy though, so if you don't like spicy food, maybe bring your own lunch. There are absolutely 0 facilities for heating or preparing food. They won't even give you hot water for any noodles you don't purchase from them. Also there are no rubbish bins on the entire hike so you'll need to bring a plastic bag to carry out your own rubbish. The toilets are pretty gross and may or may not have toilet paper so consider bringing tissues. Also the toilets generally have no sinks, so bring some hand sanitiser gel.A small towel or two to wipe away your sweat wouldn't go astray, and a warm coat/jacket and clean, dry shirt will make your time at the peak much more comfortable (addressed in a later section).We took the 781 bus from Jeju city hall at around 6.55am. We arrived at the Seongpanak stop around 7.25am.Make sure you give yourself enough time to get to the Jindallae Shelter (checkpoint around 7km into the hike) before 12.30pm. If you don't make it to the shelter before 12.30pm you will not be allowed to continue up to the peak. It's very disappointing, I'm sure, to hike for 7km, hoping to see the peak and then be told you can't go because you missed the 12.30 deadline. I can't stress this enough. At the shelter, we heard some Americans complaining that they had missed the deadline by 24 minutes (they had started the hike at 10.30am) and that there was no information available on the trail or online about this rule. They were wrong on two counts- there are at least 5 signs along the trail up to the shelter stating that you need to pass by 12.30pm (in English). Also there are a number of blogs about this hike online which also talk about the rule. Now we started at around 7.30am and made it to the shelter by 10am, but we didn't stop to rest at all before the shelter. The walk up to the shelter is 90% easy level with gentle slopes and a few short harsher sections. If you are fit enough to contemplate doing a 19.4km hike then this section should be fine for you. If you start the hike around 8.30am, you will have no issues making it to the checkpoint in time and you should make it back to the bottom by 6/6.30pm. Earlier if you don't rest too long and are relatively fit.Note: there are several places that you can stop to rest just after the shelter. If you are running close to the 12.30pm deadline, just get past the shelter and then stop to rest once you've gone past. Just make sure you don't rest too long because you've probably got another 5-6 hours before you get back to the end of the trail including the rest of the walk to the peak, and you don't want it to get dark or have to rush on the way down.The next section after the shelter is graded as 'normal' by the signs along the route. This section does have a few challenging sections but also some easier stretches as well. If you have regular short rests then it's manageable for people of minimal to moderate fitness with some huffing and puffing.The last 1-1.5km of the walk to the peak is where it starts to get difficult. By this stage you've already hiked uphill around 8km and for probably 3-3.5 hours. The way to the peak is hundreds and hundreds of stairs often with many oddly shaped rocks to navigate around whilst traversing increasingly steep steps. If you're not super fit then you will struggle on this section. At one point we were setting ourselves goals to make it up 3 sets of staircases before we would rest for 1 minute then start again. But the important point is you are so close to the top now, so just keep pushing.The top can be quite crowded. We made it by around 11.30am and hung around for about 30mins to take photos and admire the view. My next piece of advice is- bring a warm jumper because the wind is cold up there and if you're anything like me, you will be sweaty which makes the wind even colder. Another point: if you're a sweaty person, consider bringing an extra dry/warm shirt (or two) with you to change into at the top (and possibly on the way back down). If you're prone to sweat a lot, this can make a huge difference to your enjoyment at the peak because you will by dry and warm. Your photos won't look so sweaty either. Make sure you take a picture of all members of your party with the peak stone marker or the crater to prove that you reached the top.Keep in mind that the way back down can take longer than the way up because you are now passing many people on their way up and going down is very hard on your already exhausted legs and feet. It can take 4-5 hours to get back down from the peak. We started going down at 12pm and made it to the bottom by 4pm, but we stopped several times.The path is quite narrow so on your way down, you will have to stop to let people pass in the other direction many times (unless it's significantly past the 12.30pm deadline, in which case everyone will be going down). The section between the peak and the checkpoint is very hard on your feet and legs. It will feel like forever but just remember that the track gets gradually easier and gentler the closer you are to the end. Stop at the checkpoint for lunch if you haven't already had it, or you feel like some hot noodles to warm you up.Keep on all the way down, being very careful not to slip. There are many rocks and if they are slightly wet, they are very slippery. Eventually you'll make it to the bottom. Then you can take your photographic evidence of reaching the peak to the little tourist office and for 1000 won each, you'll get a certificate saying that you reached the 1950m summit of Mt Hallasan. Congratulations!Sore feet and legs and weary bodies, you can catch the 782 bus back to Jeju city for a well earned rest.

Suggest to start early, before 7am. We started at 7am, and managed to reach the summit before 1pm, but had to descend before 1.30pm. Took a total of 10 hours, up and down. Before you visit this attraction, be sure to be appropriately dressed and have the essential gear.  Hiking boots are highly recommended as the ground is uneven and mostly rock.  Sun hat and shades will also be very useful when nearing the peak as the area there is more barren without much trees.  Trekking pole will also be useful for those with knee problems.You will have to start your day early as they will disallow entry to the final stretch (at the 2nd rest point).  There are 2 rest points, both with toilets.  The 2nd rest point (higher up) sells drinks and instant bowl noodles.  Rubbish will have to be brought down and thrown when you leave the park.  I climbed in early June and there were many many many bugs and wasps at the last leg and the peak.  For those climbing during spring, please prepare some bug balm.  These are the tips;1) Start early, reach the 2nd rest stop before 12pm.  2) Have the proper gear3) If possible, have your noodles etc after you finish the peak (if you're descending via the same trail), that way, you won't have to carry your trash up the peak4) If you're driving, reach there early (before 730).  Carpark fills up pretty quick5) A mineral spring can be found along the way for cool refreshing water!

We found the reviews here very useful for preparing ourselves for the ascent so I'm contributing my own, hoping that others will find it equally helpful!   I'd say that it's a simple ascent for those already used to hill walks and there's no way one can lose the path, as it's between ropes or handrails all the way.  The path surface is mainly made of railway sleeper type large wooden beams and rocks which provide good terrain when dry.  However, for our descent it was raining and slippery and we were constantly bracing ourselves for a slip caused by the crowds - beware those with spikey walking poles! - descending more quickly than we were!  Our ascent to the peak took a leisurely 3 1/4 hours so we were delighted, although we weren't rewarded with any views but the sense of achievement and relief was great!  Our descent took 3 3/4 hours and sometimes my pace felt a little faster than comfortable, as had to concentrate so hard on each footstep placing. It looked as if some sections of the path near the summit have been replaced fairly recently, as we found it to be in good condition and not like the experience of other reviewers - and that was a relief!  I'm very glad that I wore my walking boots to protect my ankles, as the rocks are uneven and a few are slightly unstable.  So, short, if you're fit and used to hill-walking, you have nothing to fear but if you're not usually very active, then give yourself a plan B e.g. opting for the side-path to Sara Oreum if you realise, by the junction with the path off to that (round trip 40mins) that you're struggling.  That would mean that you'd still have the great satisfaction of a spectacular view from Korea's highest mountain but without the stress of having had to climb - and descend! - the 1200 metres from the bus stop to the peak!  Make sure you have enough layers of clothes and a good hat and gloves for the summit and descent, as, at this time of year, you'll definitely need them.  Oh, and if you're looking at the frequent posts with figures on alongside the path and which start with a '1' at the bottom which then progress to '2' etc, the peak is '36'.  Hoping you find this as helpful as we found other reviews!

This is my first ever hike and it was a real learning experience. Make sure to bring proper hiking shoes as the trail is VERY rocky and it can be easy to lose your footing and hurt your ankles.
